!Ventrue opponent has the same votes as me, and can also play Parity shift,
which may well be the most powerful vote ever (it won the game for him and
his ally...) !!

As Sabbat War didn't offer any equivalence that I know, wouldn't it be
necessary in the forthcoming Camarilla edition to make this vote available
to Sabbat and Independent vampires, by changing the text from "Called by any
Prince or Justicar" (which is anyway obsolete as no Inner Circle can call

>As Sabbat War didn't offer any equivalence that I know, wouldn't it be
>necessary in the forthcoming Camarilla edition to make this vote available
>to Sabbat and Independent vampires, by changing the text from "Called by any
>Prince or Justicar" (which is anyway obsolete as no Inner Circle can call
>it...)

I fear you mis-understand the term "obsolete". A number of cards were
created in Dark Sovereigns (where the Inner Circle were introduced)
which *still* only refer to Prince or Justicar. For instance,
Judgement: Camarilla Segregation.

It was clearly a design decision to limit these cards in this fashion.

However, the Rules/Design Team did alter the card older "Bloodhunt" to
take into account the Inner Circle. Had they wanted to, they could have
done similar for Parity Shift. They did not. It seems clear that it
was a design decision not to.

> to : "Called by any vampire with at least 2 Votes" ??

Some cards are limited to some sects for a certain amount of flavour and
power for that sect, or that clan, or that generation range or whatever.
It also provides a certain amount of costing, especially for cross-
discipline/cross-clan decks. A cross-clan deck will, certainly, have
more flexibility - but that comes with the price of limiting their
reliability.

On the other side, your Lasombra deck can have lots of Cardinals - one
per big vampire. My Ventrue deck can only have one Justicar out. This
gives you a far greater capacity for title based votes than me, since
you can still call Crusades (equivalent to my Praxis Seizures). And my
Ventrue can't vote on your Cardinal Benedictions, whereas I need things
like Closed Session to create the same situation (which needs a title on
the acting vampire already).

Also note that your Lasombra vampires will have, quite often, a far more
powerful discipline selection than an equivalent Camarilla vampire, due
to the Sabbat costing disparities between it and earlier sets. Tatiana
Romanova, for instance, is quite weak, in the grand scheme of things.

Your archbishops, also, can attempt to take away my titles. My Ventrue
deck can only take away the titles of Camarilla vampires (Command of the
Harpies requires a Camarilla vampire). Your Lasombra deck can take away
the titles of Sabbat vampires in a similar fashion (Excommunication).
However, it can also take away the titles of my Princes (Blood Siege),
with the added bonus that it then gets a Diocese of its own, creating a
large swing of 4 votes (I lose 2, you gain 2). (Of course, a Lasombra
deck can also use Political Struggle to achieve similar ends. This
bears less direct pressure on the current situation, which is more to do
with sect rather than clan.)

I can do things you can't; you can do things I can't. Examine,
assimilate and utilise the differences. Attempting to merely replicate
a "standard" Camarilla Parity Shift oriented deck with Lasombra isn't
going to work, they're a different clan with different sect and clan and
discipline oriented abilities. And, indeed, very, very good at what
they do.

Things which are updated by text can be found in the on-line card text

And something which hasn't been updated isn't necessarily obsolete.
Something being obsolete or obsolescent requires far more than just not
being updated.

>>

Parity Shift is "lethal" in a number of circumstances. If nothing else,
you need less pool than your opponent. This places you in an extremely
nasty danger zone if they're low, especially if they've done something
like hold back a Delaying Tactics in defence which is far from unheard
of. You've just taken yourself down to, say, 6 pool via whatever
method, to try and snag your prey who's on 7. You're now on 6 pool when
you had been planning to be on 11 (+5) with a prey on 2 (-5).

Also note that Parity Shift is, of course, limited by the number of
Methuselahs in the game, like Conservative Agitation; it becomes
progressively weaker, which can severely hamper you in the late game.

That any weenie vampires you create or influence may not be able to call
it will also seriously limit your choices. You cannot base a deck
around using it the whole time, whereas you *can* make such a decision
with Conservative Agitation or Kine Resources Contested - they function
with all vampires and don't have requirements dependent on other
Methuselahs (though ConAg depowers slowly).

Parity Shift is far from the be all and end all of votes.

>You have made very brilliantly you point : the Sabbat, as of now, have more
>possibilities to gain votes. But consider these facts :
>
>- The Camarilla supplement goes out next year, and there may be new votes
>that will do the same as the new SW or FN cards

This seems to have no relevance to the point regarding Cardinals. The
Camarilla have a specific set of titles. LSJ has specifically stated
that (whilst he is responsible for the game in the manner he is) no
Camarilla vampires will be created with titles that function like
Independent titles (votes simply stated by card text e.g. Ezmerelda).
It seems extremely unlikely that a new title worth 3 votes is going to
be created which is not unique. White Wolf are clearly interested in a
consistent back-story, so far as is possible. Creating people as
powerful as Justicars without limitations within the Camarilla has no
precedent in the World of Darkness.

In terms of vote actions, again, this has little to no relevance
regarding the generation of titles.

However, again, Sabbat War, Final Nights, Bloodlines and the Camarilla
base set are all being designed by the same group of people - White Wolf
and LSJ in chief. Were the sets being designed by one group of people,
then another group of people, then a third group of people, it seems
more likely that such duplicates may be created - a new group of
designers take a different tack on the process. A consistent set of
designers with focused goals for the game are less likely to be prone to
such mutability.

Also note National Guard Support and Reinforcements, which merely
require titled vampires. Such could have been done for any number of
other cards, had it been so wanted.

>- The Sabbat have lots, lots less titled vampires to begin with !

This all depends on how you view their focus.

The Ventrue are, of course, extremely good voters. They, between them,
have 11 titled vampires. The Brujah have 12. They're both designed to
be excellent voters. The Brujah, of course, are somewhat hampered by
the lack of Presence on the Eurobrujah, which is extremely useful for
such a deck. The Eurobrujah make up 3 of their 4 Princes (Donal,
Constanza, Volker), and have 6 Primogen.

The Lasombra have a very different time from the Ventrue. The Ventrue
are supposed to be diplomats par excellence. The Lasombra are somewhat
different. They have only 7 voters, it is true, but this from a smaller
selection of vampires total. 3 Archbishops, 2 Cardinals and Gratiano
(the 2 vote Priscus) make for an extremely powerful potential crypt.

Clearly, by design, the Lasombra are not, however, intended to be the
same clan as the Ventrue, just in a Sabbat version. Potence and
Obtenebration both provide formidable combat presence. Political
Struggle capitalises on this. The Lasombra, unlike the Ventrue, can
capitalise on their version of Archon, Templar, (which provides an
inherent rush action, though it does not provide the nicety of diablerie
freedom as in Archon). Utilising Potence, they can assemble an
extremely nasty vote and bruise deck which, executed well, is a fearsome
deck type. I've seen the Brujah execute such before now. The ability
to attack and destroy an opposing vampire in such a fashion is a
powerful ability indeed. So, you're being voted down by a Ventrue vote
deck. Political Struggle a vampire and get its votes, or simply rush
the vampire and destroy them as best you can. You have options the
Ventrue simply don't have available to them in that manner.

You also have Power Structure available to you, which is again a
significant ability. Unlike Ventrue Headquarters, this isn't a location
- useful for defence.

People don't complain that the Ventrue are betters voters than the
Gangrel. The two clans have a completely different focus. The Lasombra
have a significant voting presence, but it is far from their only
ability. They can bleed, too, though the Ventrue are better for
amassing bleed. They can fight, which the Ventrue can't.

If you're looking at a Lasombra deck and saying "I can't vote like the
Ventrue can" you've realised a fundamental point of Jyhad. If you look
at it and continue to say "I can't vote like the Ventrue but I'm going
to try anyway" you've rather missed the point.

>The
>Lasombra are the best titled, but under 8 you have nothing except one lousy

The vampires, individually, are pretty much all *good* however. The
only vampire I don't really care for is Ramiro. Gratiano probably ranks
as my favourite vampire from the entire Sabbat set. (See my Message-ID,
for instance.)

And again, you're missing the point that they're not supposed to be able
to compete with a Ventrue vote deck on equal terms, but rather on their
*own* terms.

>The "big vampires" are good, but the small ones are not !

Aaron, Cameron and Ignatio are all standard costings. (Ramiro I've
already noted I don't particularly care for. It's not that he's a bad
vampire, I would merely have preferred the original Sabbat designers to
pick something closer to, say, Gloria Giovanni - maybe OBT pot, or
something.)

Guido is fine, if you're going for something based round OBT dom - which
is perfectly sensible.

Talley, Lisette and Aurora are three good vampires. Talley is
absolutely outstanding. And then you hit the "big vampires", where I'd
tend to agree they really are quite good indeed.

So you have maybe two iffy small vampires (depending on what you choose
to build), 3 standard ones, and 3 good mid-range - more than enough to
build a deck with.

>I won't go
>over that again (it was a thread last month), but just consider that the
>first Lasombra to have even one Superior discipline costs 4, the first to
>have 2 costs 6, and all the Lasombra with the 3 disciplines in superior cost
>9 ; what is the smallest one in Ventrue ?

This is certainly true. However, it's not entirely on target, really.
Political Struggle is an excellent choice and ignores disciplines
totally. Power Structure won't care either.

Some extremely powerful Lasombra decks have been constructed with swarm
creation. Use someone big like Gratiano or someone (I'm tempted to go
for Francisco Domingo for his discipline selection and bleed, as well as
the title which is not a Camarilla praxis) to create weenie vampires
with Creation Rites. Stuff in some Embrace to allow them to create some
as well. You can also use Tribute here as serious blood/pool gain for
bringing out more vampires.

The small vampires can contribute to a war of attrition via bleed.
Dropping either Obtenebration (for stealth) or Dominate (for bleed0 is
going to be useful. And every vampire you create gives you another vote
with Power Structure. You can either use that to pass title granting
votes to them (perfectly good), or to force through key votes if you go
for a deck with more elements of something else in them. (Making the
voting issue a competent side-line, so you can get a key Banishment
passed, utilising the extra vampires for more pressure is perfectly
viable as a deck.)

Would you play a Ventrue vote deck like this? It seems unlikely. But
would you play a Toreador vote deck like a Ventrue vote deck? That also
seems unlikely. Or a Brujah vote deck? They're all different decks.
Sure, you can't do all the same things with all of them. You can mix
and match if you choose to, casting your net wide but watering down your
deck, or you can focus on their particular assets.

>I know one which has FOR, PRE and
>DOM, and 1 title, for 7 !! So, the discipline thing doesn't always work...

It's not *just* disciplines, of course. Talley's aus and +1 intercept
are terribly useful, used properly. Depending on how you choose to play
a deck, you may well prefer Gratiano's +1 bleed and 2 Prisci votes in
preference to POT. Aurora's Fortitude is really rather useful too,
combined with Lucita. And Matt Green's Lucita/Gratiano Free States Rant
deck is certainly fun and powerful.

>

demonstrating, however, that sects and clans should be played
differently, depending on what they can do.

>I'm just saying that this Camarilla
>vote has no equivalent whatsoever in Sabbat,

And how is this relevant? There are lots of things that some people can
do that others can't.

Does that fact that Tzimisce can use Haven Affinity (a card which has no
equivalent whatsoever) create inequality? No - it just gives them
something that's theirs, whereas other people have things that are
theirs.

> not to mention independants
>(but that seems more or less normal, as they're not known for voting a
>lot...).

This suggests that you've never seen a Setite Presence oriented vote

need.

Attempting to go off into "Well, I'm just addressing the sect" doesn't
help matters any; the specifics will still have the same ramifications
whether you care to address them or not.

>No, nothing, and that was my whole point. But James doesn't want to
>understand this and makes it personal. I don't.

I would suggest you're entirely wrong in this assertion; James
understands many things. Attempting to tell James what he understands
and making assumptions based thereupon is unlikely to help you ascertain
James' point of view on something. (James has no problems with
referring to himself in the third person, he does it regularly.) James
may well believe that an argument about Parity Shift which, when
challenged, then turns to "Ah, but this isn't about Parity Shift, it's
about this other thing really, I just didn't say that and expect other
people to read my mind, they just don't understand" is losing its way
and would do well to remind itself what it's trying to argue for.

There may be a larger problem in the relative power levels. However,
when we take sect wide views of power levels, we also have to take note
of the specifics, too.

Compared to the Ventrue and Brujah (two of the strongest Camarilla
voters), the Lasombra are a different kettle of fish.

Taking 2nd Tradition for the sake of argument. How much intercept do
the Ventrue have access to? Aside from the standard disciplineless
stuff available to all (newspapers, bikes, angels etc.), they have
Powerbase: Berlin, which is rarely used. None of their disciplines are
favoured with intercept. Similarly, the Brujah have access to similar
amounts of intercept, with no real discipline based alternatives. 2nd
Tradition, therefore, provides a significant boost to them, for the cost
of princes. (Of course, in the case of blocking bleed actions, the
Ventrue also have access to bleed bounce - something which both the
Lasombra and Tzimisce referred to below also do, but which the Brujah
generally lack.)

The Lasombra already have access to not insignificant amount of
intercept, relatively speaking. Darksight effectively allows permanent
intercept to be played transiently, as well as Eyes of the Night. The
Sabbat now has access to Eternal Vigilance, which provides something the
Camarilla don't have. In an environment where intercept can be light,
Eternal Vigilance may well be entirely preferable to 2nd Tradition - one
card does the work of 5 or 6 wakes (which may include 2nd Tradition).
That the Lasombra can already muster 2 intercept of their own
(Obtenebration) would mean that providing them with access to a 2nd
Tradition duplicate would significantly empower them. If they are
approximately balanced as they stand now, this would quite likely knock
game balance out by some way.

Also compare the Tzimisce, who are *without doubt* the clan with the
best access to intercept in the game - Animalism permanents combined
with Animalism untap transients and Auspex transients is extremely
powerful, in the context of intercept. Add Eternal Vigilance to the mix
and you have an extremely potent set of intercept. Do they need even
more intercept?

Such demonstrates that the Lasombra and Tzimisce voters are in a
somewhat different situation already to the Brujah and Ventrue voters;
by extension, this gives us the basic idea that was is appropriate for
them may well be inappropriate for the Sabbat, and vice-versa. If we
compare back to, say, the Toreador, we have a somewhat more even footing
to compare and contrast with. The Toreador are good intercepters,
better than the Lasombra but not as good as the Tzimisce, based purely
on their clan and discipline abilities. They do have 2nd Tradition
available to them. Such might lead us to believe that arguments above
regarding the Ventrue and Brujah are interesting but don't entirely hold
water.

However, let us recall that Jyhad is a game of many parts. Examining
intercept is all well and good, but we also have to remember what occurs
*when* we intercept one. The Ventrue can do very little to other
vampires; Pulled Fangs was disempowered some years ago, King of the
Mountain is possible but apparent and not cheap, the Island of the
Yiaros has some limited value. They can, however, defend themselves
excellently. Fortitude and Presence are both loaded with various forms
of combat defence - dodges, damage prevention, combat ends - along with
some useful side effects - untaps, minor damage.

The Brujah, by contrast, excel in offensive combat. However, they have
no source of real combat defence other than sacrificing their combat
offence. That is, in order to defend themselves, they must retreat to
effects like Strike: Dodge. Sideslip provides one small way out of
this. In order to use their own dodges, they must allow other
combatants to do so as well - they cannot play Immortal Grapple, which
is often necessary. They can do significant damage to other vampires,
but in contrast to the Ventrue, the Toreador, the Lasombra and the
Tzimisce, they lack bleed bounce in any form, thus being able to hit
back is extremely useful.

The Toreador lie between mixed extremes. They cannot defend themselves
as well as the Ventrue can - Auspex and Celerity, though they may try,
are no substitute for Fortitude (nor should they be, of course).
However, they cannot advance in combat to the extremes of the Brujah -
their celerity is useful, but needs to be combined with something. The
usual object of desire here is a gun, but these can be difficult and
expensive to obtain, relative to a transient potence strike card which
requires no pool and no equipping time. Their Sabbat brethren, of
course, have the Art of Pain available to them - 3 damage Blurred is far
from insignificant.

By contrast, the Tzimisce can do some really rather excellent combative
tricks. Carrion Crows, Song of Serenity, Blood of Acid, Horrid Form,
Skin Trap, Breath of the Dragon, Chiropteran Marauder, Body Arsenal,
Path of Metamorphosis, Inner Essence and Telepathic Tracking provide
some extremely scary offensive options. Tzimisce intercept decks
*already* do extremely well.

Lasombra have fewer intercept possibilities than the Toreador and lack
the Celerity of the Brujah for combat offence support. They manage to
slot somewhere in between the two of them on both levels. Again,
relative to the Brujah, they have bleed bounce which is far from
insignificant.

2nd Tradition is an excellent card, don't get me wrong, very useful
indeed. However, if we are, as you suggest, to look at it on a sect
based level we have to look at how it will impact numerous aspects of
that sect. Adding 2nd Tradition to the Sabbat... do we *really* want to
have Meshenka managing the best intercept in the game and cheap
offensive combat with defence possible too, even if not brilliant.

Looking at things at this sort of level allows us to see the inherent
problems with working at a sect-wide level - that it's a blanket tool,
which needs to be carefully judged. Some areas will come up to balance,
some won't be touched and others will be shifted above the balance in
that area.

There may, indeed, be a case for "filling up the corners" somewhat.
However, merely adding such cards to the Sabbat (because they're
"obsolete" to use your terminology regarding Praxis Seizure) isn't going
to help matters any. If the Sabbat are less powerful, simply
duplicating the Camarilla options isn't going to solve problems - it's
going to give them all the options they already have, all the options
the Camarilla have and one hell of a headache for people wanting to play
a balanced game.

Fifth Tradition, of course, is different. Unlike 2nd Tradition, Fifth
Tradition has very few alternatives. 2nd Tradition duplicates some
facets of the game already available to everyone (wake, disciplineless
intercept) means that a lack of it isn't chronic. (Annoying, perhaps.)
Fifth Tradition is only really mirrored by Giant's Blood and Festivo
dello Estinto, and neither of these really work in the same way.
(Though underestimating the potential utility of Festive dello Estinto
would be foolish.)

Fifth Tradition, as I have previously argued on this group, has part of
its power based firmly in the fact that it's not duplicable. It's
certainly a good card, and it's certainly doing well on an effect:cost
ratio level. There's no other real middle ground between Fifth and a
basic hunting action, though. Filling in a gap would not be an entirely
bad idea, especially if it worked in a way that big non-titled Camarilla
vampires could appreciate - we all appreciate that big vampires are not
entirely the easiest thing to play. Since the whole Fifth/Minion Tap
combo allows you to avoid putting all your eggs in one basket, it works
extremely well with large vampires.

If we look at The Fourth Tradition, it's certainly not an entirely bad
card. It would be more powerful if Govern the Unaligned and Scouting
Mission didn't provide similar and intermediary effects, and other minor
pool generators (Art Scam, Voter Captivation and so on) exist. Having a
middle ground between the base "hunt for 1/bleed for 1" effect and
Fifth's effect would not be a bad thing. But in the area of 2nd
Tradition, there is already a lot of middle ground. Giving people
another 2nd Tradition isn't going to help matters.

(Note: This is not the point you started out with, which was that the

For some value of "interesting votes". Archon (Camarilla only) is
replaced by Templar, both of which are similarly useful cards.

Anathema is gone, of course, as are a number of Camarilla oriented votes
(Command of the Harpies) which have equivalents. Kindred Restructure
can be substituted with Dramatic Upheaval - not *as* good but still very
good. The First Tradition is not available to them, but is rarely
played, being complex and extremely difficult to judge.

But let's look at the other votes still available to them. Banishment
is certainly interesting. Kine Resources Contested is one of the best
cards in the game. Conservative Agitation also has its place. Sabbat
Inquisitor - you vote to give a vampire +1 bleed, if nothing else!
Reinforcements is available to many, and very good it is too. Rabble
Razing is as effective against weenies when played by the Sabbat as it
is played by anyone else. Political Stranglehold - powerful, useful,
interesting. A well-timed Political Flux can either give you a huge
margin over what you should have or annul someone else's. National
Guard Support is potentially excellent bleed defence, especially if
you're not going for a bleed deck element at all. (And bruise and vote
will still hit *someone*). Consanguineous Boon and Autarkis Persecution
are solid pool gain, as ever. Honor the Elders is extremely useful.
Playing a fat Lasombra vote deck? Here, have three free pool to your
uncontrolled region. Disputed Territory mucks around other decks -
steal that Heidelberg, stop their blood flow. Blood Siege! Now
*there's* an interesting vote if ever I saw one. What other card in the
game can generate a permanent 4 vote swing, denying a deck access to the
Traditions its put in?

Are these cards not interesting?

Also consider the fact that votes do not always have to be used by you.
One of the most powerful factors of Legacy of Pander in its previous
mis-printed incarnation was not the fact that you could pass your own
votes but that you could shut down other people's votes. Investiture
and Cardinal Benediction can be passed excluding Camarilla vampires very
easily, no extra cards needed. You can dominate Bloodhunts and demand
that they play Closed Session just to get basic votes passed because you
can generate a large number of votes, if you're so inclined. You can
then use them for your own votes, too. Of course, there are no
interesting votes that the Sabbat can call. Oh no.

>to mention that I began the game with Sabbat War and lack most of the
>Camarilla cards ; but should I try to play votes when it doesn't seem to be
>able to win (well, at least it's fun to play, but...) ?

Sure, you're welcome to try it. Lots of fun ideas can come out of "Hey,
let's see if I can..." and then sticking together a deck with a number
of moving parts. The out-of-turn Malkavian Rotschreck deck is one such
deck.

Can the Lasombra play votes? Sure. Can they do it as a pure tactic?
That's less obvious. The Gangrel, say, are not the world's most obvious
voters. Sure, they can muster a prince or two if they have to, but you
wouldn't say they suck just because they can't pass votes. It's not
their role to. If you realise that the Lasombra are good voters without
being superb at it, and capitalise on what the Lasombra actually *are*
rather than what you would *like* them to be, you can have a blast.

Have a look at, say:

"Tournament Winning Deck: Praxis Seizure: College Station (4vps in final
round) July 14th, 2001 by Jeffrey Thompson" on <URL:http://www.thelasomb
ra.com/decks/twd.htm> A very good deck, combining a number of factors
previously outlined. A powerful vote deck that goes a different way to
your standard Camarilla vote deck, creating weenies, "wasting" actions
on bringing out other vampires with Scouting Mission and Govern (which
can, of course, should you so wish be used as bleed cards if they turn
up in the late game).

Or: "Crusade: Seattle, Continental Championship Seattle Qualifier,
Winning Deck by Jeffrey Thompson March 2001" Again, this takes a
different tack, mixing and matching Presence in their as well to provide
an unexpected twist.

Or: "Michael Eichler's Winning Deck Portsmouth December 2000, Lasombra
on the Presidental Lawn (Sabbat War variant), Crypt [avg = 6.31]" A
deck with voting power, sure, but mixed in with bleed bounce, with
bleed, with combat and so on. Again, very different from how you'd play
a similarly themed Camarilla deck - perhaps closest to a Brujah deck.

>> KRC/Conservative Ag. Domain Challenge and Ancilla
>> Empowerment really if you
>want to do any harm through votes.
>
>Don't forget Transfer of Power and, Conservative Agitation, and, if you can

Or for the fact that you're playing a different deck. If you can play a

>But it's the whole question I'm asking here : do the conceptors at

>the Sabbat to be able to play a true voting deck, or would it just be a
>little "plus" in mostly discipline-based decks ?

For some values of "true", the Sabbat already can.

However, the Sabbat were not designed to be a hugely powerful
influential political force. That's why they have other options
available to them - for instance, why the !Toreador have Art of Pain
instead of anything else.

>> The Camarilla should always have an advantage in the political > arena

In terms of the strategy game, the Sabbat are doing pretty well at the
moment, if you know how to play them well.

That they have been compensated in other areas (though opinion may
differ as to whether it was enough or not) would suggest that just
giving them the same options voting-wise is going to mean that the other
options will seriously empower them on top of that.

>> Their sect-only cards are more suited for groups,
>

Blood Feast - works better with lots of vampires. In terms of pool
generation, this has potential use as an alternative to Fifth/MT.

Festivo dello Estinto - to get the maximum use, you probably want to
have a lot of vampires out to use it all there and then.

Shock Troops - generates those groups, potentially. Difficult to use
well.

The Sabbat is very much based around the idea of a pack mentality.

The Ventrue can defend themselves, certainly. They cannot *fight*
however.

If you play the deck well, you can win. You can call a vote and make
sure it gets called. You may have a slightly harder time passing it
initially, because your set-up may take a little longer. Them's the
breaks, as they say. No-one is good at everything. If the Lasombra had
stealth, combat ability, bleed and unstoppable votes, crikey.

>But not only the votes are inferior (compare 3rd tradition and Creation

Happy to, though do recall they're not votes. For a potentially wider

Is this necessarily inferior? You'd need to make a convincing argument,
because of the fact that the cards are different.

I'm not sure how it was established that they can't fight. That seems
a bit like saying the Brujah can't fight. They have a costless dodge
with additional strike, a costless maneuver (granted, not as good as
Flash), can deal hand damage at long range, if they can't manage to
keep it close and the opponent doesn't S:CE (many decks have taken it
as enough to simply maneuver to long versus the potence deck and have
cut down a little on the density of S:CE).

OBT is not *quite* the combat discipline that CEL is, but it's not bad
either. Dominate is a better discipline than Presence for everything
but voting and S:CE, and the Lasombra have Power Structure for votes,
and OBT for S:CE. Overall, I really don't see the perceived weakness
of the Lasombra compared to the Brujah. They're not the fighters that
Nossies are, they're not the voters than Ventrue are, and they're not
the stealth bleeders that the Malkavs are. But they seem to
approximately match the Brujah in all categories, and are better then
them at stealth bleed.

Lasombra play as a somewhat toolboxy deck. You can play a focused
deck with them, but their strenghts are varied, and it's hard to take
advantage of them all.

I haven't read the whole thread yet, but it seems like maybe you want
the Lasombra to be able to do politics on par with Ventrue, but the
Sabbat is not a political sect. Presence is a Camarilla Discipline
(in my personal WOD campaigns, the !Tor have aus/cel/vic, and the !Bru
have cel/obt/pot), as political maneuverings and kindred society games
are just not a part of the Sabbat. You are not voted into power, you
wrest that power in a bloody takeover. That said, I *do* think there
should be better Sabbat only cards that are more combat oriented. We
have a few already, but a lot of them are too weak, compared to the
Camarilla equivalent. I took out the Blood Feasts and War Party from
my Lasombra deck, not because I couldn't play them, but just because
they were never ever useful and were just clogging up my hand.

I don't think that better vote cards are the way to go, though.

playing with a CL houserule may make certain cards appear stronger
than they really are...

Yes, I have been opposed by other good votes decks with Camarilla vampires
in tournaments that I have won. Some of the things that allow Sabbat vote
decks to beat Camarilla vote decks are as follows:

An (almost) Autopass vote to gain votes that generates other
votes that pass automatically. (Cardinal Benediction followed by
Cryptic Rider and any other vote - Blood Siege is particularly appropriate
in this third card slot.)

Having permanent votes on the table. The clans I vote with in tournaments
(Lasombra, Tzimisce, Tremere Antitribu) can all gain and support large
quantities of vampires with three votes.

Private Audience can cause all of your votes to pass without opposition,
as the other players, especially if playing Camarilla vote, cannot vote
much more often than not.

-Closed Session isn't as good, as right now there are many more Camarilla
voters in the tournament scene than Sabbat or Independent voters, so isn't
included in most Camarilla voting decks.

Playing the table or metagame against itself. The Camarilla vote players
that I beat with the Sabbat voting decks didn't play the table or the
metagame as well as I did in those particular tournaments.

In general, the deck that calls (and passes) more votes will win, regardless
of the sect of their vampires. Therefore making the votes palatable to
possible cross-table allies is much more important in the beginning until
you can gain vote lock while voting. No winning vote deck has to have
vote lock on offense and defense, but it must be able to pass 90%+ of the
votes it does call.

As an aside:

There is no vampire in the game that is worth more than three
pool in the long run. Decks that vote and Minion Tap/Fifth have
to split their stealth and their actions among voting and Fifthing.
Sabbat decks can simply take the pool with the first Minion Tap,
rely on their strong combat, and not ever bother to replace the blood.

>would you prefer to go 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th or 5th?

Depends on what kind of deck I'm playing, and depends on my opening
crypt. If I'm playing a weenie deck, I want to go 1st or 5th; the
"first action" is critical, but it's also nice to be able to turn over 4
vampires behind a person who has none at all yet.

If I'm playing a big-fatty deck, it depends on the fatty I want first.
If my crypt is Ambrogino, Marianna, Carlotta, and Paul diCarlo, I can
make arguments for wanting to be in EACH position.

1st: I get Ambrogino on turn 3 with no significant loss of time.
Alternatively, I get Carlotta AND Paul on turn 3.
2nd: I get Paul diCarlo immediately and have a minion who can act.
3rd: I get Carlotta on turn 2.
4th: I get Marianna on turn 2.
5th: I get Marianna on turn 2.

Now, which seating position is BEST for me depends totally on what my
deck is designed to do, and what is sitting near me. If I'm a
"govern-backwards" deck, I would LOVE to be in the 1st slot; I can get
my oldest vampire out, Govern to Carlotta, and have a second fatty on
turn 4. If I'm a "beat things up" deck, I probably want Paul ASAP, and
Carlotta soon after.

So IMO, the "seating position" scheme is quite balanced, though there is
a small ambiguity between 4th/5th at most tables.

--
Derek

>Are you talking about balance between the
>players, the cards, the clans, the disciplines or what?

Cards, decks, players.

Cards - Individual cards have relatively small effects. More important to have
a good deck than to play a good card.

Decks - What are the tier 1 decks in V:TES? Is tier 1 a meaningful concept in
V:TES? Isn't the variety of the winning decks notable? I've played lots of
crap decks and they can get VPs because of a favorable situation. I've played
good decks that didn't get any. More important to manage a game well than to
have the best deck, assuming you can even figure out what the best deck is.

Players - Multiplayer games allow for ganging up on the leader. Free for all
multiplayer games suffer for this as all the game comes down to is ganging up
on the leader until someone sneaks victory through or everyone else has
exhausted too many resources to keep battling. V:TES rewards focusing on
specific players; it has partial victories (underrated and unexamined, IMO).
To a much greater degree than other multiplayer CCGs, from what I've seen, it
remains stable when played well by most or all of the players. Note that I say
most because, while one sided games are very possible, rarely does one bad
player cause them.

Then how are
>you measuring it? And which CCGs are you comparing it with?

All of them, though it should probably only be compared to other multiplayer
CCGs as multiplayer CCGs are inherently more balanced. Which do you consider
better balanced?

Orpheus asked what metagame means.

The metagame is the game around the game.

Do I take a voting deck that works in local play to
a tournament in another state?

The decisions on this are based on what you think
the current metagame is (or will be). What type of
decks exist, what type of counters to your own deck
exist and whether or not they can reasonably be
expected to show up.

The metagame also describes the drift in a group.

A group might start out with no one playing votes,
everyone playing some form of bleed or combat deck.
As one player decides to do a serious vote deck,
the metagame changes. What you need to put in your
decks changes, in this example, you now need to
include vote defense.

As more people in that group add vote defense, or
switch to voting themselves, the player cognizant
of the metagame will switch to something different.

Richard Garfield wrote an article or two on the
concept of the metagame in early issues of the
Duelist.

If you are interested in the topic, you might search
back issues, or search WOTC's website.

http://www.wizards.com

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott

Orpheus wrote:
> Ok, now I'll really pas for an ignorant, but I must confess... I don't know
> what everybody means by : "metagame" !!

"Metagame" was a term that was originally coined by board gamers to discuss
issues around things gamers do that may be counterproductive in terms of
winning the game currently being played but may help their interests in future
games. The classic example was a player in a multiplayer game who felt he'd
been doublecrossed or otherwise abused, disrespected, ganged up on, or whatever
by some other player he had hoped to get better treatment from and therefore
decided to sacrifice any chance he had for winning the current game in order to
torpedo the other player's chances of winning - e.g. by sending his entire force
to attack that player and leaving his home territory undefended against a third
player. The perceived benefit would be to gain a reputation as someone who other
players would do well to avoid upsetting in future games.

In CCGs, the term refers to a different aspect of play: choosing a strategy at
deckbuilding time. Since this is done by each player without knowledge of what
deck they're going to be playing against, it's considered important that any
CCG have no "pure strategy" - which is a term used in games theory. A "pure
strategy" is one that is either superior or at worst equal to all other strategies
available, meaning that intelligent players would always prefer to use it to
optimize their chances of winning. A CCG with no pure strategy leaves it to
players to guess what other players will choose in order to decide which strategy
they themselves should choose. (A CCG with a pure strategy is no fun, obviously.
No interesting choices to be made.) Players who succeed at outguessing their
opponents and choosing the most advantageous strategy in a game or tournament are
said to have "won the metagame". The term is analogous to the board game use of
the same term (discussed above) since in both cases, strategy decisions are made
with no single game in mind but with overall success over many games being the
consideration.

Fred
